paragraphs.145: The Eulogio “Amang” Rodriguez Institute of Science and Technology (EARIST) provides the institutional setting for this research-management study. Current research policies, required forms, and decision responsibilities should be confirmed with the Cavite Campus. An older manual retained in the project is reserved for a separate institutional compliance check; it is excluded from this manuscript’s dated literature base pending approval of an exception to the reference-age requirement.
paragraphs.182: To document current campus research-administration practices and requirements through authorized interviews, observation, and current institutional documents, distinguishing those requirements from the features already implemented in the software;
paragraphs.192: To evaluate selected product-quality characteristics—Functional Suitability, Interaction Capability, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Security—using ISO/IEC 25010:2023 as the proposed evaluation basis, combining respondent assessments with relevant technical observations; and
paragraphs.205: Location / Organization: The intended institutional setting is EARIST Cavite Campus. Current institutional research policies and any claimed equivalence with OVPREIS forms require confirmation by the appropriate campus personnel. The older archived manual is not treated as an automatically approved exception to the literature-date requirement.
paragraphs.241: Evaluation Boundary: Planned participants are administrators, research staff, faculty users, and students associated with the study setting. Only evaluated tasks, modules, user groups, and conditions may support conclusions. The questionnaire must be aligned with the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics before data collection; no previously approved or completed instrument is assumed. Institutional baseline findings, respondent counts, and quality ratings are not supplied in these chapters.
paragraphs.264: Institutional Research Guidelines: Campus-authorized policies, forms, and procedures used to validate requirements. The applicable version and any exception for an older institutional source must be confirmed before it is cited in the final manuscript.
paragraphs.266: ISO/IEC 25010:2023: The product-quality model used as the proposed evaluation basis in this revision. Five characteristics are selected for the study; the selection is not a complete assessment of the model or a certification claim.
paragraphs.269: OVPREIS Forms: Institutional research forms relevant to requirements validation. Their current versions and applicability must be confirmed; complete digitization and routing equivalence are not assumed.
paragraphs.294: Brooks and McCormack (2020) distinguish digital information, changes to operating processes, and wider institutional transformation. This helps frame RMS as an intervention whose organizational effects still require evaluation.
paragraphs.297: Presentation: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide the forms, record views, role navigation, and progress indicators. Nixon (2021) covers these web-development technologies. Their use in RMS is established by the project files; a book’s coverage of additional libraries does not establish that those libraries are installed.
paragraphs.311: Smirnova and Tezuysal (2022) address practical MySQL work, including queries, joins, and administration. Such operations are relevant to connecting researcher, project, chapter, review, and output records. In RMS, the implementation and schema establish the actual record relationships; retaining version and decision history remains a requirement to verify.
paragraphs.312: The inspected RMS uses MySQLi prepared statements. This is an implementation finding rather than a feature inferred from a textbook or database brand. Prepared queries do not replace ownership checks, explicit action permissions, server-side input validation, or controlled file access. These behaviors require separate verification in the application.
paragraphs.317: Veve (2021) examines thesis/dissertation submission workflows involving an institutional repository and ProQuest. The study distinguishes review, metadata, access restrictions, and publication processing. These concerns help organize RMS repository evaluation without implying that it implements ProQuest integration or the same workflow. Ahammad (2021) further identifies metadata and structural quality control as repository-management concerns.
paragraphs.321: Brooks and McCormack (2020) treat digital transformation as coordinated organizational change. For RMS, responsibilities, user preparation, and operating conditions therefore need attention alongside the application itself.
paragraphs.322: Campus-specific claims require campus-specific evidence. Interviews, observations, and current authorized institutional records should establish how the Cavite Campus manages research. Published experience from other settings can inform the investigation but cannot establish local delays, paper consumption, or record-loss rates.
paragraphs.326: The proposed evaluation selects Functional Suitability, Interaction Capability, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Security from ISO/IEC 25010:2023 (ISO/IEC, 2023). This focused selection addresses the intended RMS tasks; it does not assess the entire model. The methodology and questionnaire must use the 2023 terminology consistently. Interaction Capability replaces the former product-model heading Usability; existing questionnaire items cannot be assumed equivalent without review.
paragraphs.329: Interaction Capability: Observe representative users learning the interface, recognizing suitable functions, operating controls, and recovering from input mistakes. Collect structured assessments and task observations, including errors and assistance needed. Final questionnaire items and their mapping to the selected model require review before data collection.
paragraphs.336: Veve (2021) studies workflows for submitting graduate theses and dissertations to institutional repositories and ProQuest. The published abstract covers deposit, review, metadata, restrictions, and distribution. It supports distinguishing repository processing from manuscript development. For RMS, archive discovery, document access, and title/chapter decisions should be evaluated as related but separate functions.
paragraphs.338: Le, Shar, Bianculli, Briand, and Nguyen (2022) present a framework for recovering and checking role-based access policies in web applications. The institutional research record identifies policy validation and access-control defect detection as its purpose. This informs RMS checks of intended rights and direct requests. RMS does not implement the study’s automated framework, and its results cannot be transferred to RMS.
paragraphs.342: Brooks and McCormack (2020) examine digital transformation in higher education. Their distinction between operational digitalization and wider change supports separating implemented RMS capabilities from institutional adoption and measured benefits.
paragraphs.346: Granić and Marangunić (2019) review TAM applications across educational technologies and users. Their abstract identifies perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as important acceptance constructs. This recent review informs RMS user questions, although a research-administration system differs from a teaching platform. It does not establish acceptance at EARIST.
paragraphs.357: Current campus research policies and forms must be obtained or confirmed through the appropriate institutional office. The project’s archived manual can support a separate policy comparison if an exception to the date rule is approved. It is not included in the recent-reference bibliography, and its contents do not establish present campus practice.
paragraphs.361: The contribution proposed here is an implementation and evaluation of an EARIST-oriented RMS with shared student/faculty submissions, permission-controlled decisions, preserved versions, sequential chapters, and associated research records. It is not a claim that no comparable system exists. Literature and study summaries in this revision use verified publications from 2018–2026; an access date is not substituted for an unknown publication date.
paragraphs.368: Table 2.1 compares research-management and repository workflows described in recent publications with the inspected RMS. External capabilities are limited to the cited abstracts or institutional records. The comparison does not establish procurement costs, superiority, or institutional compliance without corresponding evidence.
paragraphs.370: The comparison includes two Philippine research-management platforms, an electronic-thesis/dissertation workflow study, and an electronic research-ethics system. These address different institutional tasks. Their submission and review functions should not be described as identical to RMS’s title-and-chapter sequence. The comparison is based on dated research sources rather than undated product overviews or unsupported absent-feature claims.
paragraphs.390: TAM provides an acceptance perspective using perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Granić and Marangunić (2019) are cited as recent reviewers of educational applications, not as the model’s originators. The planned RMS instrument must operationalize the selected constructs.
paragraphs.398: Application Processing: PHP handles authorization, validation, uploads/downloads, locked submissions, version capture, and review decisions. Following the access-policy verification focus of Le et al. (2022), tests should compare implemented rights with intended permissions.
paragraphs.405: Functional Suitability, Interaction Capability, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Security organize the proposed evaluation. The final methodology must justify this selection, map questionnaire items and technical checks to the 2023 model, and document actual results. This revision updates the planned framework; it does not alter an existing dataset or claim that an earlier instrument has already been revalidated.

ARCHITECTURE AND AUTHORIZATION
Browser presentation → PHP processing → relational persistence.
